messages.author: f4c2e63aec3c6db2
messages.subject: transparent BUGS transpilation
parts:
Hi all,

I was surprised to see some code in Richard McElreath's Statistical
Rethinking that translates from BUGS into Stan.

Here's an example from https://github.com/rmcelreath/rethinking

```r
library(rethinking)

f <- alist(
y ~ dnorm( mu , sigma ),
mu ~ dnorm( 0 , 10 ),
sigma ~ dcauchy( 0 , 1 )
)

fit <- map(
f ,
data=list(y=c(-1,1)) ,
start=list(mu=0,sigma=1)
)
```

At first I was a bit dismayed to see this. After some reflection it
occurred to me that for simple models CmdStan/RStan/PyStan could
transparently detect BUGS code and, in simple cases, just translate it
directly into Stan code (replacing all the obvious distributional
BUG-isms with appropriate Stan replacements). It would throw an error on
any complicated models but if it worked on 90% of simple BUGS/JAGS
models I think it might be welcomed by users as they transition to Stan.

This could also make sense as a stand-alone website where you paste in
your BUGS/JAGS code into a form. The site would spit out Stan code (or
an error if it can't translate the code), along with helpful annotations
about helpful changes.

Best,

Allen

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] transparent BUGS transpilation
parts:
To translate a BUGS model to Stan, you need to know which
variables are data and which are parameters and you
need to know the shape (not size) of the data objects.
So McElreath must be using the formula list and data to convert
the BUGS-like spec.

McElreath must be leaning on R's internal formula syntax
for expressing a BUGS program as a sequence of formulas.
To do this outside of R would require a parser for BUGS.

BUGS also has deterministic nodes.

And there's also JAGS, which is slightly different syntactically.

We support most, but not quite all of the features of the
BUGS/JAGS languages --- they'd be easy to add (like
interpolation and the F distribution).

- Bob

I suppose I like the idea of a `pandoc` for probabilistic programming
languages. It would be cool to be able to go back and forth between
arbitrary language pairs (with simple models).

And I also can't help but take McElreath's map2stan as a critique of the
language+interface as it currently exists!

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] transparent BUGS transpilation
parts: For the distribution names, I don't get why he uses the R/Bugs conventions of dnorm, dcauchy, etc., rather than Stan's normal, cauchy, etc. It can't be that dnorm is easier to understand than normal (the actual name of the distribution). Unless the goal is for people to never move beyond rethinking and into Stan, why not just use Stan's distribution names, which typically correspond to the actual names of the distributions?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] transparent BUGS transpilation
parts:
I think the "re" in "rethinking" comes from this point
McElreath makes on his site:

The book is aimed at PhD students and researchers in the natural
and social sciences.

This audience has had some calculus and linear algebra,
and one or two joyless undergraduate courses in statistics.
I've been teaching applied statistics to this audience for
about a decade now, and this book has evolved from that experience.

I'd like to write a book aimed at replacing that joyless undergrad
class with something at the level of Gelman and Hill.

- Bob
